passages.t: Not silent for Zion's sake, and new names
passages.happening:
‘For Zion’s sake I will not keep silent, and for Jerusalem’s sake I will not keep still, until her righteousness shines like a bright light, her salvation like a blazing torch’ (verse 1).

The nations will see her righteousness and kings her glory. She will be called by a new name that the LORD himself will give (verse 2). ‘You will be a crown of glory in the hand of the LORD, a royal diadem in the palm of your God’ (verse 3).

‘No longer will you be called Forsaken, nor your land named Desolate’ (verse 4). She will be called Hephzibah, and her land Beulah, ‘for the LORD will take delight in you, and your land will be His bride’ (verse 4). ‘And as a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, so your God will rejoice over you’ (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 62 completes the bright center of the last part of Isaiah. Chapter 60 described Zion's glory, chapter 61 the anointed one who brings it, and chapter 62 a voice that will not rest until the promise is kept. Who is speaking is not said: the prophet, the anointed one of chapter 61, or God himself. Interpreters differ.

For the returned exiles, the names Forsaken and Desolate described what they saw every day. Jerusalem stayed partly in ruins for decades after the return. Nehemiah describes its walls broken and gates burned as late as the middle of the fifth century BC.

Names mattered in Israel. A change of name marked a change of who someone was, as with Abram and Jacob. Hephzibah says that the speaker's delight is in her, and it was a real name: the mother of King Manasseh was called Hephzibah. Beulah means married. In a world where an abandoned woman had little security, to be called married was to be called protected and honored.

The word for marry, baal, also named the Canaanite god Baal. Isaiah reclaims it for the LORD's covenant love, as in 54:5.
passages.later: Abram was given a new name with a new future: ‘your name will be Abraham, for I have made you a father of many nations’ (Genesis 17:5). The name Hephzibah was carried by a queen of Judah: ‘His mother’s name was Hephzibah’ (2 Kings 21:1).
passages.asks: God gives a new name to a city that was called Forsaken. Ask what name you have carried that God does not call you. And ask what it would mean for you that God delights in his people the way a bridegroom delights in his bride.

passages.t: Watchmen who give God no rest
passages.happening:
‘On your walls, O Jerusalem, I have posted watchmen; they will never be silent day or night’ (verse 6). Those who call on the LORD are to take no rest, ‘nor give Him any rest until He establishes Jerusalem and makes her the praise of the earth’ (verse 7).

‘The LORD has sworn by His right hand and by His mighty arm’ (verse 8). He swears that he will never again give their grain to their enemies or let foreigners drink the wine they worked for (verse 8). Those who harvest the grain will eat it and praise the LORD, and those who gather the grapes will drink the wine in his holy courts (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
Watchmen stood on city walls to look for danger or messengers, calling out day and night. Here they become people of prayer who call on the LORD without stopping. They are told to give God no rest, a bold picture of prayer that will not let go of a promise.

The promise about the harvest spoke to people who had watched foreign armies, and later imperial taxes, take the fruit of their labor. Nehemiah records people borrowing to pay the king's tax. The law had warned that a foreign people would eat the produce of the land. God swears by his right hand that this curse will end.
passages.later: The law had warned, ‘A people you do not know will eat the produce of your land and of all your toil’ (Deuteronomy 28:33). Nehemiah's people confessed that their harvest went to the kings set over them (Nehemiah 9:37).
passages.asks: The watchmen are told to give God no rest. Ask what promise of God you have stopped praying for. And ask whether you have watched someone else take the fruit of your labor, and how this oath might speak to that.

passages.t: Prepare the way: your Savior comes
passages.happening:
“Go out, go out through the gates; prepare the way for the people!” (verse 10). “Build it up, build up the highway; clear away the stones; raise a banner for the nations!” (verse 10).

The LORD has proclaimed to the ends of the earth what is to be said to Daughter Zion: her Savior comes, his reward is with him, and his recompense goes before him (verse 11).

‘And they will be called the Holy People, the Redeemed of The LORD; and you will be called Sought Out, A City Not Forsaken’ (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
The highway and the raised banner picture preparations for a royal arrival or a great procession, when roads were cleared of stones and flags marked the route. The chapter gathers threads from across the book: the highway of 40:3 and 57:14, the watchmen of 52:8, and the reward that comes with God from 40:10.

The word for Savior in verse 11 is the word for salvation, yesha. The names Joshua and Jesus are built from it.

The chapter is framed by silence refused (verse 1) and a city no longer forsaken (verse 12). After it, chapter 63 turns sharply to judgment and to the people's lament, showing that the promised glory has not yet fully arrived.
passages.later: Matthew joins the opening words of verse 11 with Zechariah 9:9 when Jesus enters Jerusalem: ‘See, your King comes to you, gentle and riding on a donkey’ (Matthew 21:5). The highway was first called for in Isaiah 40:3.
passages.asks: The city once called Forsaken is now called Sought Out. Ask whether you think of yourself as forsaken or as sought out by God. And ask what stones in the road you could clear for someone else to come home.
